Juliana General remark: the battery cannot "decide" whether to charge from the public grid or the PV. (there is no separate cable from the battery to the public grid vs. to the PV. there is just 1 cable connecting the battery to the wiring of the microgrid.) The battery is communicated a setpoint, i.e. a single signed value (+/-/0). negative value -> charge positive value -> discharge 0 -> idle Example: When the battery is set to charge 10 kW, it will charge 10kW. If the PV at this point in time produces 1kW, then it will charge 1kW from PV & 9 kW from the public grid. If the PV at this point in time produces 0kW, then it will charge 10kW from the public grid.

step.name:
Battery controlling: The battery is communicated a setpoint, i.e. a single signed value (+/-/0). negative value -> charge positive value -> discharge 0 -> idle Example: When the battery is set to charge 10 kW, it will charge 10kW. If the PV at this point in time produces 1kW, then it will charge 1kW from PV & 9 kW from the public grid. If the PV at this point in time “produces” 0kW (so PV produces nothing), then it will charge 10kW from the public grid.
Bottom: (Deep discharge Protection) Condition: Battery charge is below 10%. Target: Protect the battery and keep it at a safe charge level. Action: If NetDemand is lower than GridLimit, the battery is primarily charged via the public grid until the NetDemand is equal to the GridLimit. In this state to prevent a critical state of charge. Sensors monitor whether there is insufficient PV power available (and tbd later if the grid price is favourable to ensure a reliable supply). Also, we want to look at the composition of the public grid’s energy mix (eco-friendly and reduce CO2 production). The battery does not discharge, it cannot be used for e-car chargers. If NetDemand is higher than GridLimit, the battery is not charged, the battery is set to idle, grid is already too loaded.
Low: Condition: Battery charge is between 10% and 70%. Action: In this state, the battery is charged primarily via the public grid if NetDemand is less than GridLimit. When there is PV power being produced, then the battery might also be charged (partially) with PV power. If NetDemand is greater than GridLimit, the energy stored in the battery is also used to charge the chargers for electric cars. (= peak shaving). In other words: the battery is set to discharge to serve the additional power needed from the EV-chargers. Ff the NetDemand is lower than the GridLimit, the battery would be charged via the public grid until the NetDemand is equal to the GridLimit, similar to when the battery charge is below 10%. Target: Balance between self-consumption, PV utilisation and grid consumption Further Consideration: The system enables dynamic switching between PV surplus operation and grid supply—particularly when public electricity prices are favorable or demand changes occur—and also considers the eco-friendly composition of the public grid (energy mix), such as the share of solar, gas, or wind power, to decide when and how much to charge the battery.
Medium: Condition: Battery charge is between 70 % and 90 %. Target: Optimise surplus energy for load shifting (Peak Shaving) When high battery charge levels (> 70 %) are reached, the discharged portion should be directed to the consumers (e.g. e-car charger) in order to smooth load peaks. Action: In this average state, there is a dynamic change depending on the current PV generation, (later: current electricity prices). Here, the system can decide whether to feed from PV surpluses, draw grid power or switch to peak shaving by battery discharging. If NetDemand is negative,meaning there is excess PV production, we use that excess energy to charge the battery. If NetDemand is between 0 and GridLimit, then battery is idle (does not charge and is not used) If NetDemand is greater than GridLimit, the battery is used for discharge until NetDemand is equal to GridLimit again (peak Shaving).
High: Condition: Battery charge is 90 % or higher. Action: In this state, the battery is mainly used to smooth peak loads (peak shaving) and to support e-car chargers, for example. High PV generation or favourable grid conditions favour remaining in this state.
Electricity price variability: A dynamic price signal (time-of-use tariffs, real-time prices, etc.) should be integrated into the control logic. This allows the system to discharge the battery more in phases with high prices (peak loads) and charge it preferentially in phases with low prices - and also considers the composition of the public grid (energy mix), such as the share of solar, gas, or wind power, to decide when and how much to charge the battery.

Overload oder nicht? NetDemand_kWh= (CarLoad_total_kW - PVCons) * 0.1 Overload = NetDemand_kWh > GridLimit_kWh_per_cycle Overload = 4.0 kWh > 2.5 kWh → True 1: Kontrolle über die Ladeleistung die Ladung auf das GridLimit beschränken und dadurch Overload vermeiden und Kosten sparen.
  • reduziere die CarLoad prioritätsbasiert
  • → dadurch bleibt NetDemand ≤ GridLimit
Oder: nicht die Nennleistung (CarLoad) der Wallboxen ändern, sondern einfach: Die tatsächlich zugewiesene Energie pro Cycle begrenzen → langsamere Ladung · Eine Wallbox kann z. B. 22 kW, aber temporär nur 4.4 kW zuteilen · Das Auto lädt dann langsamer, aber ohne Unterbrechung 2: keine Kontrolle (z. B. alle Autos laden „dumm“ mit voller Leistung) ❌ Dann zahlt man für alles über dem GridLimit einen teureren Tarif, Netz evtl instabil

PV1 Wenn mit 4 kW PV Strom geladen wird: Ein Akku mit 60 kWh wäre in 15 Stunden voll. Mit 11 kW wären es nur etwa 5,5 Stunden.
Also Akku/PV1 = Stunden und, Akku/(PV1*10)= Anz (6 Minuten) Zyklen
Energiebedarf / (Leistung × 10) ergibt die Anzahl der 6-Minuten-Zyklen zur vollständigen Ladung.
cycle_duration_h = 0.1 # 6 min = 0.1 h car["power"] * cycle_duration_h # ergibt kWh pro Cycle
